titleStmt.title: Exact analysis for basic single-rate cyclic executives

analytic.title: Exact analysis for basic single-rate cyclic executives

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: The academic interest in cyclic executives for multitasking in hard real-time systems decreased significantly during the past decades. Moreover, cyclic executives are hardly addressed in contemporary text books, if at all. Cyclic executives are still in use, however, and there is therefore a need for analysis techniques for these executives.

In this document, we consider two basic cyclic executives, i.e. a single-rate AFAP (as fast as possible) and a single-rate timedriven AFAP cyclic executive, scheduling a given sequence of independent hard real-time polling tasks in a single-processor system. We present exact analysis for both cyclic executives and discuss their relative strengths and weaknesses in terms of jitter, energy efficiency, and schedulability. Unlike existing approaches, which typically take periodic tasks as a starting point for cyclic executives and focus on schedulability of tasks, we take the schedulability of the system as a starting point, i.e. whether or not the system meets its deadlines. In particular, we do not assume periods and deadlines for tasks.

div.head: A. Background and motivation
div.p: As described in [1], cyclic executives are generally used in defense military systems and traffic control systems to handle periodic tasks. Cyclic executives effectively execute hard realtime tasks in a continuous loop, in which every task appears at least once. Since the paper by C. Douglass Locke [2], in which it is concluded that the fixed-priority approach generally dominates the cyclic executive approach for hard real-time systems, the academic interest in cyclic executives has gradually decreased 1 . Accordingly, cyclic executives are mentioned in contemporary text books, such as [1], [4]- [6], but hardly addressed in detail. Despite the decreasing academic interest, cyclic executives are still in use, however. In a recent survey of 120 industry practitioners in the field of real-time embedded systems [7], it was observed that from the 97 respondents to the question which task scheduling policy/policies are used in the considered systems, 54.17% answered "static cycle/table driven/time-triggered". Availability of exact analysis for cyclic executives therefore remains desirable. This document is a treatise on exact analysis for basic single-rate cyclic executives scheduling independent, hard real-time polling tasks in singleprocessor systems.

div.head: B. Problem description
div.p: Hard real-time systems require timely responses to events. As illustrated by an airbag, a system response (the inflation of an airbag) shall be provided in a well-defined interval relative to the occurrence of an event (a collision), i.e. neither too early nor too late. A system specification may therefore constrain the time-interval from an event to a response by both a lower bound, a so-called best-case system deadline, as well as an upper bound, a so-called worst-case system deadline. For hard real-time computing systems, where control is realized in software, these system deadlines give rise to timing constraints on the real-time tasks that have to detect events (through regularly polling sensors) and provide responses (using actuators).

In this document, we assume a hard real-time system with a set of n (input) events, a set of n (output) responses, and a 1-1 relationship between events and responses. Events are sporadic, i.e. are characterized by a minimal inter-arrival time. Each event-response tuple is characterized by a best-case system deadline and a worst-case system deadline, where the worst-case system deadline is at most equal to the minimal inter-arrival time of the event. Each event-response tuple is handled by a dedicated real-time polling task. A task detects an event through observation, e.g. by reading sensory data, and provides a response through a command, e.g. using an actuator; see Figure 1. We assume a single-processor system and a basic singlerate cyclic executive to schedule the set of tasks. In particular, we assume a statically known sequence of tasks executed in a continuous loop, in which every task occurs exactly once.
div.formula: System S τ 1 τ 2 τ n ...
div.p: Each task is characterized by a lower bound and an upper bound on its computation time, i.e. by a best-case and a worstcase computation time. Although tasks scheduled by means of a cyclic executive are typically assumed to be periodic [8], i.e. are typically assumed to be activated with a fixed interarrival time (or period), we do not make that assumption in this document. The problem addressed in this document is how to determine the schedulability of the system, i.e. whether or not the best-case and worst-case deadlines of the system are met. Part of the problem concerns the derivation of timing constraints for the tasks from the deadlines of the system.

div.head: C. Contributions
div.p: In this document, we consider two basic single-rate cyclic executives, an AFAP (as fast as possible) and a time-driven AFAP cyclic executive. We assume that the sequence of jobs to be executed in a cycle is known. We present exact analysis for both cyclic executives and discuss their relative strengths and weaknesses in terms of jitter, energy efficiency, and schedulability.

div.head: D. Organization
div.p: The remainder of this document is organized as follows. In Section II, we present a basic real-time system model. The problem is formalized in Section III. Exact best-case analysis, which turns out to be trivial for cyclic executives, is also addressed in this section. In Section IV, we provide a recap of the basic single-rate cyclic executives considered. Exact worst-case analysis of these basic cyclic executives is the topic of Section V. The relative strengths and weaknesses of these cyclic executives are discussed in Section VI. We conclude the document in Section VII.

div.head: II. A BASIC REAL-TIME SYSTEM MODEL
div.p: We assume a system S, a set E S of n sporadic (input) events e 1 , e 2 , . . . , e n , a set R S of n (output) responses r 1 , r 2 , . . . , r n to these events, and a 1-1 relationship between events and responses. Each event e i is characterized by a minimal interarrival time WT S i . Each event-response tuple < e i , r i > is characterized by a best-case system deadline BD S i and a worstcase system deadline WD S i , where 0 ≤ BD S i ≤ WD S i ≤ WT S i . Moreover, we assume a set T S of n independent polling tasks τ 1 , τ 2 , . . . , τ n , where task τ i senses event e i and provides response r i . Each task τ i is characterized by a best-case computation time BC i and a worst-case computation time WC i , where 0 < BC i ≤ WC i . The execution of a task is termed a job. A job of task τ i is denoted by ι i,k , with 0 ≤ k, i.e. the first job of τ i is denoted by ι i,0 . The computation time C i,k of every job ι i,k of task τ i shall be between BC i and WC i , i.e.
div.formula: ∀ 1≤i≤n ∧ 0≤k BC i ≤ C i,k ≤ WC i .
div.p: We use a i,k , s i,k and f i,k to denote the activation time, start time and the finalization time of job ι i,k , respectively. The response-time R i,k of job ι i,k of task τ i is now defined as
div.formula: R i,k def = f i,k -a i,k .(1)
div.p: The best-case response time BR i and worst-case response time WR i of τ i are subsequently defined as
div.formula: BR i def = inf 0≤k R i,k ,(2)
div.p: and
div.formula: WR i def = sup 0≤k R i,k ,(3)
div.p: respectively. The start jitter SJ i of a task τ i is defined as the maximum deviation of the start-times of a task from a strictly periodic pattern, i.e.
div.formula: SJ i = sup 0≤k ∧ 0≤ ((s i,k -k × T i ) -(s i, -× T i )) , (4
div.p: where T i denotes the (assumed) period of the task. We assume that tasks are scheduled by cyclic executives, run non-preemptively and do not suspend themselves. The sequence of tasks executed in a cycle is assumed to be known statically. Moreover, we ignore scheduling overhead and system initialization. When a system S meets all its deadlines under a specific cyclic executive and a specific sequence of tasks, the system S is called schedulable under that cyclic executive and that sequence.
For ease of presentation and without loss of generality, the jobs of tasks in a cycle are assumed to be executed in the order of increasing index, i.e.
div.formula: ∀ 1≤i<j≤n ∧ 0≤k s i,k < s j,k .

div.head: III. PROBLEM FORMALIZATION
div.p: As described in Section I-B, the response r i of a hard realtime system S to the occurrence of an event e i at time t e shall be provided in a well-defined time-interval, bounded by a bestcase system deadline BD S i and a worst-case system deadline WD S i relative to the occurrence of the event; see Figure 2 We assume a real-time task τ i that regularly polls for the event e i and provides the response r i upon the occurrence of the event. In this section, we derive timing constraints for task τ i for two cases. The first case, addressed in Section III-A, recapitulates the existing approach for strictly periodic tasks, where a period T i and a best-case task deadline BD i and a worst-case task deadline WD i are derived from the system

div.head: A. Strictly periodic polling tasks -a recap
div.p: In this section, we derive timing constraints for strictly periodic polling tasks from the system deadlines and formulate both worst-case and best-case schedulability conditions for tasks as well as the system.

1) A worst-case schedulability condition: For a strictly periodic polling task τ i , a worst-case situation arises when (i) the event occurs immediately after a job ι i,k of τ i polls for the event, (ii) job ι i,k immediately starts upon its activation, (iii) the next job ι i,k+1 experiences a worst-case interference of other tasks, and (iv) job ι i,k+1 requires its worst-case computation time for execution; see Figure 3. For such a worst-case situation, ι i,k+1 must finish before the worst-case system deadline WD S i . Based on Figure 3, we therefore derive the following timing constraint for task τ i based on activation and finalization times
div.formula: ∀ 0≤ f i, +1 -a i, ≤ WD S i . (6
div.p: For a strictly periodic polling task with period T i , this can be rewritten to

div.p: Hence, by using (3), ignoring system initialization, and choosing the period T i and worst-case task deadline WD i of task τ i such that (see also Figure 3)
div.formula: T i + WD i ≤ WD S i (7

div.formula: ∀ 1≤i≤n T i + WD i ≤ WD S i ∧ WR i ≤ WD i . (8
div.p: As long as the period T i and deadline WD i of the task τ i satisfy this constraint, and τ i is guaranteed to meet its deadline WD i , the system deadline WD S i is met as well. Observe that no specific values for the period and deadline are required, i.e. many tuples satisfy (8). A specific selection of values is to decide upon a so-called implicit deadline, where the period and worst-case task deadline are equal, i.e. T i = WD i . In such a case, (8) simplifies to

3) Concluding remarks: From the previous subsections, we conclude that a system S, based on (i) strictly periodic polling tasks to handle events and (ii) cyclic executives executing tasks non-preemptively, meets its deadlines when the following schedulability condition holds
div.formula: ∀ 1≤i≤n T i + WD i ≤ WD S i ∧ WR i ≤ WD i ∧ (BC i ≥ BD i ≥ BD S i ) . (11
div.p: How to check the condition falls outside the scope of this document.

For real-time systems, various types of tasks are typically distinguished based on their activation pattern or constraints on the inter-arrival time of jobs. Well-known examples include periodic tasks, with a fixed inter-arrival time of jobs, sporadic tasks [10], with a minimal inter-arrival time of jobs, and elastic tasks [11], with both a minimal and maximal inter-arrival time of jobs. The constraint expressed by Equation ( 7) for a polling task does not specifically correspond to any of these basic task types, because the period T i is essentially a maximal interarrival time of jobs.

We finally observe that the so-called minor cycle and major cycle, which are typically used to describe a (multi-rate) cyclic executive [1], are generally derived from the periods of the tasks. In particular, the minor cycle and the major cycle are generally taken to be the GCD and the LCM of the periods of the tasks, respectively.

div.head: B. A "regularly" polling task
div.p: Although it is common to assume periodic tasks for system scheduled by means of a cyclic executive, there is no inherent need to do so. In this section, we derive timing constraints for "regularly" polling tasks from the system deadlines and formulate both worst-case and best-case schedulability conditions for both the tasks and the system.

1) A worst-case schedulability condition: Similar to a strictly periodic polling task τ i , a worst-case situation arises for a "regularly" poling task when (i) the event occurs immediately after a job ι i,k of τ i polls for the event, (ii) job ι i,k immediately starts upon its activation, (iii) the next job ι i,k+1 experiences a worst-case interference of other tasks, and (iv) job ι i,k+1 requires its worst-case computation time for execution; see Figure 5. For such a worst-case situation, ι i,k+1 must finish before the worst-case system deadline WD S i . Based on Figure 5, we therefore derive the following timing

3) Concluding remarks: From the previous subsections, we conclude that a system S, based on (i) "regular" polling tasks to handle events and (ii) cyclic executives executing tasks non-preemptively, meets its deadlines when the following schedulability condition holds
div.formula: ∀ 1≤i≤n ∀ 0≤k f i,k+1 -s i,k ≤ WD S i ∧ BC i ≥ BD S i . (15)
div.p: The best-case schedulability condition is independent of a specific cyclic executive and checking the condition is considered trivial. In the remainder of this document, we therefore focus on checking (13) for various basic single-rate executives, where the sequence of tasks to be executed in a cycle is assumed to be known.

div.head: C. Problem formulation
div.p: As illustrated in this section, exact best-case analysis of a system S, where scheduling is based on a cyclic executive with non-preemptive execution of tasks, is trivial. We therefore focus on exact worst-case analysis in the remainder of this document.

For a (worst-case) deadline WD S i of the system S, related to event e i ∈ E S , we have to guarantee that task τ i ∈ T S provides a timely response r i ∈ R S . We therefore have to make sure that for all tasks τ i the length of the interval from the start time s i,k of a job ι i,k till the finalization time f i,k+1 of the next job ι i,k+1 is at most equal to WD S i ; see (12). To determine worst-case schedulability of the system S, we therefore have to prove (13).

IV. A RECAP OF BASIC SINGLE-RATE CYCLIC EXECUTIVES For (basic) cyclic executives, tasks can simply be implemented as procedures and executed within a loop. A single-rate cyclic executive essentially executes every task exactly once in a cycle. In the following subsections, two basic types of single-rate cyclic executives are presented, single-rate AFAP and single-rate time-driven AFAP. A single-rate AFAP cyclic executive has at least two general disadvantages. A first disadvantage is that tasks may experience drift2 , which is generally considered undesirable. We will illustrate this by considering the start times of jobs of a task τ i . The start time s i,k of job ι i,k can be bounded by

div.head: A. Single-rate AFAP cyclic executive
div.formula: s 1,0 + k × 1≤j≤n BC j + 1≤j<i BC j ≤ s i,k ≤ s 1,0 + k × 1≤j≤n WC j + 1≤j<i WC j . When 1≤j≤n BC j < 1≤j≤n
div.p: WC j , the length of the interval in which job ι i,k may be started becomes arbitrary large for increasing k. Stated differently, task τ i experiences unbounded start jitter or drift.

A second general disadvantage is that a single-rate AFAP cyclic executive is energy inefficient, because the processor is constantly active executing tasks. The single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive, described in the next subsection, resolves both these disadvantages.

div.head: B. Single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive
div.p: For a single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive, a cycle is started by a timer. The sum of the worst-case computation times of all tasks shall be less than the inter-arrival time T S of the timer, otherwise the (worst-case) executions of the tasks do not 'fit' in a cycle, i.e.
div.formula: 1≤i≤n WC i ≤ T S . (16
div.p: Figure 8 illustrates such a cyclic executive with cycle time T S , where the cycle is started at time Φ, i.e. the start time of the first job of task τ 1 is given by s 1,0 = Φ. The start time s i,k of job ι i,k is now bounded by
div.formula: s 1,0 +k ×T S + 1≤j<i BC j ≤ s i,k ≤ s 1,0 +k ×T S + 1≤j<i WC j .
div.p: The length of the interval, in which job ι i,k may be started, is now bounded by a value that is independent of k. Stated differently, task τ i experiences (bounded) start jitter. The start jitter SJ i of task τ i is given by
div.formula: SJ i = 1≤j<i (WC j -BC j ) .
div.p: The time-driven AFAP cyclic executive therefore resolves the first disadvantage of the AFAP cyclic executive. By starting cycles with an inter-arrival time of T S , the spare time, i.e. the combination of slack3 and gain time 4 , can be used to execute background tasks or run the processor at a lower, more energy efficient, clock frequency after the cycle is completed. The second disadvantage of the single-rate AFAP cyclic executive is therefore also resolved by this executive.

div.head: V. EXACT WORST-CASE ANALYSIS
div.p: In this section, we first revisit the general exact condition for the worst-case schedulability of a system S when tasks are scheduled by a basic cyclic executive. We subsequently present two example systems, which we will use in the remainder of the section for illustration purposes. Next, we consider analysis for each of the two basic single-rate cyclic executives.

div.head: A. Jitter
div.p: As described in Sections IV-A and IV-B the single-rate AFAP cyclic executive gives rise to drift, i.e. unbounded jitter, whereas the single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executives only gives rise to bounded jitter.

div.head: B. Energy efficiency
div.p: As described in Section IV-A, the single-rate AFAP cyclic executive is energy inefficient. To address the relative strength of the single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive, we determine bounds on the fraction of time that can be gained for background processing by that cyclic executive compared to a single-rate AFAP cyclic executive.

div.head: C. Schedulability
div.p: For reasons of lack of space, we merely present a theorem regarding schedulability. We refer the interested reader to [13] for the proof of Theorem 3 and an example illustrating that the AFAP cyclic executive can schedule a task set that the time-driven AFAP cyclic executive cannot. Theorem 3. From a scheduling perspective, the single-rate AFAP cyclic executive dominates the single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive.

div.head: VII. CONCLUSION
div.p: In this paper, we considered scheduling of independent polling tasks on a single processor using two basic single-rate cyclic executives, i.e. an AFAP and a time-driven AFAP cyclic executive. Unlike existing approaches that typically assume periods and deadlines for tasks, we focussed on whether or not the deadlines of the system are met. A major advantage of our approach is that there is no need to decide upon the specific periods and deadlines of the tasks to determine schedulability of the system.

We addressed the following two main topics. Firstly, we presented exact analysis for these two basic cyclic executives. Because best-case analysis turned out to be trivial, focus of this paper has been on exact worst-case analysis (Theorems 1 and 2). We showed that the exact worst-case analysis for a single-rate time driven AFAP cyclic executive requires both worst-case and best-case computation times of tasks. Secondly, we investigated the relative strengths and weaknesses of these two cyclic executives, and found that they are incomparable. On the one hand, a time-driven AFAP cyclic executive outperforms an AFAP cyclic executive when jitter and energy efficiency are considered. We presented a method to determine the maximum cycle time for a timedriven AFAP cyclic executive (see Theorem 2), aiming at maximum energy efficiency. On the other hand, the AFAP cyclic executive dominates the time-driven AFAP cyclic executive from a schedulability perspective (see Theorem 3). We observed that the schedulability test of the time-driven AFAP cyclic executive depends on the order of the tasks in the cycle. An optimal task ordering algorithm falls outside the scope of this paper, however, and is a topic of future work.

Focus in this paper has been on two basic single-rate cyclic executives. Exact analysis for other types of cyclic executives and a discussion on the relative strengths and weaknesses of these executives are topics of future work.
